title: Jeremiah 9:1–11
context: Versification: English 9:1 is Hebrew 8:23, and English 9:2–26 is Hebrew 9:1–25; this page keeps the WEB numbers. The unit opens with a voice of grief, usually read as Jeremiah’s own lament for “the daughter of my people,” though some readers hear the prophet’s sorrow merging with the LORD’s. In 9:3–9 the LORD speaks, marked by “says the LORD,” exposing a society saturated with lies, where neighbors and brothers cannot be trusted. He announces that he will “melt” and “test” his people. The first-person weeping in 9:10 is again hard to assign with certainty, and 9:11 is the LORD’s word that Jerusalem will become heaps. Both traditions read the passage as covenant judgment spoken with grief, not with cold detachment.

verses.text: Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a spring of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah wishes his head were waters and his eyes a spring, so he could weep day and night for the slain. Arminian readers see a prophet whose grief shows how deeply he longs for his people’s repentance and rescue.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet’s tears as fitting sorrow for judgment he must announce yet does not enjoy. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of a messenger who weeps over the very people he must warn.

verses.text: Oh that I had in the wilderness a lodging place of wayfaring men, that I might leave my people and go from them! For they are all adulterers, an assembly of treacherous men.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah wishes for a lodging place in the wilderness to escape his people, for they are adulterers and treacherous. Arminian readers note the tension: the prophet weeps for them and yet longs to leave them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the verse the strain of faithful ministry among a people unfaithful to God. Both traditions read the image of adultery as covenant unfaithfulness, and they note that grief and weariness can live together in a faithful servant.

verses.text: “They bend their tongue, as their bow, for falsehood. They have grown strong in the land, but not for truth; for they proceed from evil to evil, and they don’t know me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the people bend their tongues like bows for falsehood and do not know him. Arminian readers note that their refusal to know God is presented as a moral choice that grows into a settled pattern.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the root of the lies in a failure to know the LORD, so that corrupt speech flows from a corrupt heart. Shared ground: both traditions read knowing God as covenant relationship, not mere information.

verses.text: “Everyone beware of his neighbor, and don’t trust in any brother; for every brother will utterly supplant, and every neighbor will go around like a slanderer.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD warns everyone to beware of neighbors and brothers, since each will supplant and slander. Arminian readers see how unfaithfulness to God breaks down trust among people, spreading through families and communities.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the word supplant, which may recall Jacob’s name and story, though the text does not make that link explicit. Both traditions read the verse as a portrait of social collapse when truth is abandoned.

verses.text: Friends deceive each other, and will not speak the truth. They have taught their tongue to speak lies. They weary themselves committing iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: Friends deceive each other and have taught their tongues to lie, wearing themselves out in iniquity. Arminian readers note the phrase taught their tongue: lying has become a learned habit, cultivated by repeated choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the exhausting labor of sin: people weary themselves pursuing what destroys them. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that sin enslaves and tires those who practice it.

verses.text: Your habitation is in the middle of deceit. Through deceit, they refuse to know me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the people live in the middle of deceit and through deceit refuse to know him. Arminian readers stress the word refuse, which presents their ignorance of God as willful resistance, not mere lack of light.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the refusal and see a heart that suppresses knowledge of God through deceit. Both traditions agree that the people are responsible for refusing to know the LORD, and that deception isolates them from him.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD of Armies says, “Behold, I will melt them and test them; for how should I deal with the daughter of my people?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says he will melt and test his people, asking how else he should deal with them. Arminian readers see refining judgment aimed at purifying, with God’s question showing his reluctance and care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the metallurgical image as God’s sovereign work of purging, judging the dross while preserving a people for himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the refining as judgment with a purpose, not mere destruction.

verses.text: Their tongue is a deadly arrow. It speaks deceit. One speaks peaceably to his neighbor with his mouth, but in his heart, he waits to ambush him.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says their tongue is a deadly arrow, speaking peace while the heart lies in ambush. Arminian readers note the gap between outward words and inward intent, a hypocrisy the LORD sees and names.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as exposing a divided heart, saying one thing and plotting another. Both traditions read the image of the arrow as showing how deceitful speech wounds, and how God judges motives as well as words.

verses.text: Shouldn’t I punish them for these things?” says the LORD. “Shouldn’t my soul be avenged on a nation such as this?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks whether he should not punish them and be avenged on such a nation. Arminian readers see God’s justice responding to persistent, chosen evil after repeated warnings, which the people ignored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rhetorical question as affirming that God’s holiness requires judgment on unrepentant sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the question as showing that judgment is just and not arbitrary, as God himself reasons with his hearers.

verses.text: I will weep and wail for the mountains, and lament for the pastures of the wilderness, because they are burned up, so that no one passes through; Men can’t hear the voice of the livestock. Both the birds of the sky and the animals have fled. They are gone.
verses.arminianNotes: A voice says it will weep and wail for the mountains and pastures, burned and empty of livestock and birds. Arminian readers note that the speaker is uncertain, either the prophet or the LORD, and that the creation itself suffers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise allow either speaker and see the desolation of the land as a sign of covenant judgment. Both traditions read the lament as grief over what is lost, and they do not press the speaker’s identity beyond what the text makes clear.

verses.text: “I will make Jerusalem heaps, a dwelling place of jackals. I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will make Jerusalem heaps and a home for jackals, and Judah’s cities desolate. Arminian readers see the fulfillment of covenant warnings given long before, now reaching their sobering end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as the one who brings judgment through historical events such as the Babylonian conquest (compare 2 Kings 25). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as God’s sovereign word over Jerusalem’s coming ruin.
